source: Zhao et al. (2025) Absolute Zero: Reinforced Self-play Reasoning with Zero Data
finding: One model proposes its own tasks, scored by learnability (neither too easy nor unsolvable), then solves them with a code executor as verifier. No human data. This is machine deliberate practice: self-set goals, instant feedback, rising difficulty.
numbers: AZR-Coder-7B beats the prior best 7B zero-setting model by 1.8 points on overall average, and beats models trained on expert human code data by 0.3 on coding average. Math gain after code-only training: +10.9 (Base-7B) and +15.2 (Coder-7B) vs +0.65 for expert code models. Gains by size: 3B +5.7, 7B +10.2, 14B +13.2.
limits: Only code-executable tasks; learnability uses the solver's own rollouts. Absolute gains are modest.
agent_relevance: Strongest AI analogue of deliberate practice. Our agent does not train, but the learnability rule (pick tasks the solver gets right about half the time) can pick which probe tasks to run.

source: Bae et al. (2025) Online Difficulty Filtering for Reasoning Oriented Reinforcement Learning
finding: Proof and tests that learning signal is largest at success rate 0.5. Prompts with pass rate 0 or 1 give zero gradient. Balanced filtering (keep mid-difficulty) beats plain GRPO; skewed filtering is worse than plain.
numbers: Qwen2.5-7B, five math benchmarks: plain GRPO avg 26.3 in the main table; balanced filtering over 30 (up to +10 points on AIME) in under half the steps; avg rises from 27.3 at pass-rate window (0,1) to over 30 at (0.3,0.7). Abstract: up to +12% gain.
quote: selecting tasks of intermediate difficulty maximizes learning efficiency
limits: Needs many rollouts per prompt to estimate pass rate. Math only. Table numbers differ between model setups.
agent_relevance: Machine counterpart of the rising-difficulty ingredient: too easy and too hard both teach nothing. Fits G1: spend effort only where the outcome is uncertain.

source: Zhang, Arora, Mei, Zanette (2025) SPEED-RL: Faster Training of Reasoning Models via Online Curriculum Learning
finding: Adaptive curriculum picks prompts of intermediate difficulty after a cheap screening phase; the gradient signal-to-noise ratio improves.
numbers: 2x to 6x faster wall-clock training to the same target accuracy across RL algorithms and benchmarks; no accuracy loss.
limits: Speedup is in training compute, not final accuracy. Screening costs extra inference.
agent_relevance: Difficulty targeting changes efficiency, not ceiling. Same pattern as human deliberate practice.

source: Yu et al. (2025) DAPO: An Open-Source LLM RL System at Scale
finding: Dynamic sampling drops prompts whose group accuracy is exactly 1 (and 0), since they give zero advantage and no gradient. Keeps only informative prompts.
numbers: DAPO reaches 50 points on AIME 2024 with Qwen2.5-32B base, vs 47 for DeepSeek-R1-Zero-Qwen-32B, using 50% of the training steps. Naive GRPO reached 30.
limits: Dynamic sampling is one of four techniques; its separate share is shown only in an ablation figure.
agent_relevance: Already-mastered items are wasted practice. Skip mastered, retry the mid-difficulty ones.

source: Kimi Team (2025) Kimi k1.5: Scaling Reinforcement Learning with LLMs
finding: Uses curriculum sampling (start easy, move to hard, pass rate as difficulty proxy) plus prioritized sampling on failed problems. Ablation shows curriculum sampling beats uniform sampling.
numbers: Headline: 77.5 AIME, 96.2 MATH500, 94th percentile Codeforces. Curriculum ablation shown as curves on Omni-MATH500, AIME2024, MATH500; no single number read.
limits: Curriculum effect shown only as curves; mixed with other recipe choices.
agent_relevance: Frontier labs already use train-on-what-you-fail, the machine form of focusing on weak spots.

source: Huang et al. (2025) R-Zero: Self-Evolving Reasoning LLM from Zero Data
finding: Challenger is rewarded for questions where the Solver is maximally uncertain (reward = 1 - |2p - 1|); Solver trains on them. Co-evolving curriculum from zero data.
numbers: Qwen3-4B-Base math average 42.58 to 49.18 over three iterations (+6.49 as reported; iter 1 48.44, iter 2 49.07, iter 3 49.18). General-domain +7.54. Gains shrink each round and some sub-scores fall at iter 3 (MATH 79.8 to 78.0, GSM8K 92.12 to 89.08).
limits: Pseudo-labels come from majority vote, so label noise grows as questions get harder. Returns diminish.
agent_relevance: Mirrors the human finding that gains flatten. Self-set difficulty needs a verifier or noise grows.

source: Zhou et al. (2025) Self-Challenging Language Model Agents
finding: Agent plays challenger (writes a task with instruction, verification function, pass and fail cases), then executor, trained with RL. Test cases filter bad tasks.
numbers: Over two-fold improvement for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on M3ToolEval and Tau-Bench with only self-generated data (abstract). Self-improve baselines without the task filter did much worse in the same table.
limits: Weak 8B starting point; two benchmarks.
agent_relevance: The quality gate on self-made practice tasks is the key piece; matches G3 (pass must be checked on something independent).

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager: An Open-Ended Embodied Agent with Large Language Models
finding: LLM agent loop with automatic curriculum (next task from current state), skill library, and iterative prompting with execution errors and self-verification. No weight updates.
numbers: 3.3x more unique items, 2.3x longer distances, milestones faster by 15.3x (wood), 8.5x (stone), 6.4x (iron); only agent to reach diamond. Ablations: random curriculum cuts discovered items by 93%; no self-verification cuts 73%; GPT-3.5 instead of GPT-4 gives 5.7x fewer items.
quote: Automatic curriculum is crucial for the agent's consistent progress
limits: Minecraft only; GPT-4 black box; self-verification sometimes wrong.
agent_relevance: A deliberate-practice loop run entirely in a prompt scaffold, no training. Curriculum plus verified feedback are the two big pieces.

source: Matiisen et al. (2017) Teacher-Student Curriculum Learning
finding: Teacher picks the task where the student's learning curve slope is steepest (learning progress) and re-picks tasks where performance is dropping, to stop forgetting.
numbers: Abstract and introduction read; per-task numbers not extracted.
limits: Pre-LLM RL setting.
agent_relevance: Older formal version of practice at the edge with revisit of decaying skills; a rule the program, not the model, could run.

source: Dennis et al. (2020) Emergent Complexity and Zero-shot Transfer via Unsupervised Environment Design (PAIRED)
finding: An adversary designs environments that maximize the protagonist's regret, giving solvable but hard tasks. Fixes domain randomization (no adaptation) and minimax adversaries (unsolvable worst cases).
numbers: Abstract read: adaptive curricula and better zero-shot transfer than both baselines in grid tasks (figures not extracted).
limits: Grid and navigation tasks, not language.
agent_relevance: Names the failure of too-hard practice: unsolvable tasks give no signal.

source: Silver et al. (2017) Mastering Chess and Shogi by Self-Play with a General RL Algorithm (AlphaZero)
finding: Self-play with clear win/loss feedback against an equally strong opponent (itself), from rules only. Opponent strength rises with the learner.
numbers: Beat Stockfish in chess after about 4 hours (300k steps), Elmo in shogi in under 2 hours; superhuman in all three games within 24 hours.
limits: Perfect-information games with exact rules and a free simulator.
agent_relevance: Cleanest machine case of goals, instant feedback, repetition and rising difficulty. Shows deliberate practice works best where feedback is exact.

source: Lightman et al. (2023) Let's Verify Step by Step
finding: Step-level human feedback (process supervision) trains better reward models than final-answer feedback. Active learning picks the most convincing wrong solutions to label.
numbers: Best-of-1860 on a MATH subset: process reward model 78.2% vs outcome reward model 72.4% vs majority voting 69.6%. Active learning about 2.6x data efficiency. 800,000 step labels (PRM800K).
limits: Feedback is human-labelled and costly; math only.
agent_relevance: Matches the claim that specific, immediate feedback beats outcome-only feedback. Supports checks that locate the failing step (G2).

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Feedback helps only when it is external. With oracle labels self-correction looks great; with the model's own judgement it hurts.
numbers: GPT-3.5 with oracle: GSM8K 75.9 to 95.5; HotpotQA 26.0 to 49.0. Intrinsic, GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 after round 1 (41.8 after round 2); GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0 over rounds.
limits: GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 on three datasets; later models may differ.
agent_relevance: Practice on own feedback is not deliberate practice. Feedback must come from code or ground truth. Supports G2 and G3.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
finding: Agent keeps a text memory of reflections on failed attempts and retries: attempt, feedback, reflection, retry, no weight updates.
numbers: HumanEval pass@1 91% vs GPT-4 80%; absolute gains over baselines 22% on AlfWorld (12 iterative steps), 20% on HotPotQA, 11% on HumanEval.
limits: Relies on test or oracle signals; Huang et al. show gains vanish without them.
agent_relevance: Prompt-only repetition with feedback. Useful only when the failure signal is real.

source: Madaan et al. (2023) Self-Refine: Iterative Refinement with Self-Feedback
finding: Same model drafts, critiques and rewrites, repeated. No training.
numbers: About 20% absolute average improvement over 7 tasks with GPT-3.5 and GPT-4; code optimization +8.7 over base GPT-4; quality tends to rise with more iterations.
limits: Largest gains on subjective tasks; Huang et al. report reasoning tasks without external feedback do not improve.
agent_relevance: Contested evidence; use only with an external check on the feedback.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Tutor CoPilot: A Human-AI Approach for Scaling Real-Time Expertise
finding: Preregistered randomized trial: an LLM gave live expert-style hints to human tutors. Tutors with it asked more guiding questions and gave away fewer answers.
numbers: 900 tutors assigned (450/450; 782 at launch: 386 treatment, 396 control), 1,800 K-12 students. Mastery +4 percentage points (p<0.01); +9 points for students of lower-rated tutors. About $20 per tutor per year. 550,000+ messages analysed.
limits: Math tutoring, one provider; outcome is topic mastery, not long-run skill.
agent_relevance: LLM-delivered feedback can improve human practice; background only for our agent.

source: Scarlatos et al. (2025) Training LLM-based Tutors to Improve Student Learning Outcomes in Dialogues
finding: Tutor model trained by DPO to maximize a simulated student's chance of a correct next answer, with a pedagogy rubric in the loop.
numbers: Student-correctness prediction improved 33% over the next best method (GPT-4o). Student model AUC 0.76 on MathDial test. Correctness weight 0.5 to 0.75 kept rubric quality.
limits: Outcome is predicted correctness from a simulated student, not real learning.
agent_relevance: Trade-off: optimizing only correct answers can erode teaching quality; a small correctness weight kept it.

source: Macnamara, Hambrick, Oswald (2014) Deliberate practice and performance in music, games, sports, education, and professions: A meta-analysis
finding: Human meta-analysis: deliberate practice explains only part of performance variance, varying by domain.
numbers: From memory, not opened: about 12% overall, 26% games, 21% music, 18% sports, 4% education, under 1% professions.
limits: Not opened; figures unverified.
agent_relevance: Human baseline: machine analogues work where feedback is exact (games, code, math), the same domains where human DP works best.

source: Ericsson, Krampe, Tesch-Romer (1993) The role of deliberate practice in the acquisition of expert performance
finding: Founding violin study; best group had about 10,000 hours of accumulated practice by age 20.
numbers: From memory, not opened: about 10,000 vs 7,800 vs 3,400 hours for best, good, teacher groups.
limits: Retrospective self-report; not opened.
agent_relevance: Definition used by the machine papers: self-set goals, immediate feedback, tasks at the edge of ability.

source: Bengio et al. (2009) Curriculum learning
finding: Original ML claim that easy-to-hard ordering speeds learning and can improve the final solution.
numbers: Not opened.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Root of the curriculum results above.

source: Zelikman et al. (2022) STaR: Self-Taught Reasoner
finding: Loop: generate rationales, keep those that reach the right answer, fine-tune, repeat. For failures, rationalization: give the correct answer as a hint and ask for a rationale. Early machine form of practice with outcome feedback.
numbers: CommonsenseQA: +35.9% over few-shot baseline, +12.5% over a model fine-tuned to answer directly, 72.5% vs 73.0% for a fine-tuned model 30x larger.
limits: Needs ground-truth answers as the feedback; rationalization can produce post-hoc rationales.
agent_relevance: Retry-on-failure with the answer revealed is a form of worked-example feedback.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager: iterative prompting ablation
finding: Second Voyager finding: feedback types in the prompt loop each matter. Self-verification decides when to move on or retry a failed task.
numbers: Removing self-verification: -73% discovered items. Voyager is built on GPT-4 with no fine-tuning; skill library plus curriculum is what compounds over 160 prompting iterations.
limits: Self-verification occasionally fails to recognise success.
agent_relevance: Moving on versus retrying should be a code-checked rule, as in G1.

source: Bae et al. (2025) Online Difficulty Filtering: skewed filtering
finding: Keeping only easy or only hard prompts (skewed filtering) does worse than no filtering. The benefit is specific to the middle band.
numbers: Table 2 (Qwen2.5-7B): SFT avg 37.3; GRPO plain family around 39.6 with 0-to-1 filter; balanced windows reach higher on AIME (13.1 to 15.0) and AMC (41.0 to 47.0).
limits: Table partly garbled in text extraction; read as approximate.
agent_relevance: Both ends of difficulty are wasted practice, as in the human zone-of-proximal-development claim.

source: Zhao et al. (2025) Absolute Zero: pass@k and general reasoning
finding: After self-set practice the model keeps answer diversity: at pass@256 and 512 it matches or beats the base model in 4 of 5 cases, with one exception at AIME24 (k=512). Higher average on MMLU-Pro than comparison models.
numbers: pass@k up to 512 on three coding and two math sets; AZR-Base-7B better or equal in 4 of 5.
limits: Self-play on code only.
agent_relevance: Practice on self-made tasks did not collapse diversity, unlike a worry that RL narrows reasoning.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Cannot Self-Correct: multi-round decline
finding: More self-correction rounds without external feedback do not help; some get worse.
numbers: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 75.1 to 74.7 (1, 3, 5 calls); GPT-4 HotpotQA 49.0 to 49.0 to 43.0; GPT-4 CommonSenseQA 82.0 to 79.5 to 80.0.
limits: Prompts follow the source papers; different prompts could change numbers.
agent_relevance: Repetition alone is not practice; limit retries unless a real signal changes.
